summary: Describes what client applications need from real-time communication services, such as audio and video conferencing. It is an informational memo asking for discussion, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: This is a wish list of what programs need from the network to run live calls well.

questions: what are the requirements for real-time communication services
how do you specify delay bounds
how do you translate requirements across network layers
subtitle: What applications need from networks to deliver live audio, video, and time-sensitive data

tldr.problem: Applications like videoconferencing and live audio need guarantees about delay, throughput, and reliability. Traditional best-effort networks make no promises and cannot support these applications well.
tldr.mechanism: Clients should specify their performance requirements (delay bounds, throughput minimums, reliability needs) and properties like sequencing and failure recovery. The network commits to meeting these specs through a contract.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes a framework for specifying real-time requirements and translating them across protocol layers, with examples for voice, video, datagrams, and file transfer.

today: RFC 1193 is an Informational RFC that remains unobsoleted. It predates the widespread deployment of QoS mechanisms in the Internet (which came much later with MPLS, DiffServ, and other technologies). The framework it proposes influenced later work on quality-of-service specification, though the Internet took decades to implement the kinds of guarantees the RFC calls for.

sections.title: Why Real-Time Services Matter
sections.content:
A real-time communication service is one where clients can specify their performance needs and the network promises to meet them. Traditional Internet best-effort service offers no guarantees; packets may be delayed, lost, or reordered. For video streaming, VOIP, or emergency alerts, this is not good enough. The RFC defines real-time service as involving a contract: the server promises to deliver a certain level of performance, and the client promises to follow certain rules. If the network fails to deliver, the server pays a penalty (though the RFC does not define what that penalty would be).

The RFC argues that as networks start to offer guaranteed-performance services, demand will grow beyond expectations. This is because availability of high-quality services induces new applications that depend on them. The examples cover digital video and audio, urgent messages in distributed systems, database queries, and file transfers.
sections.eli5: Imagine if the post office could promise: this letter will arrive tomorrow, and if it does not, we pay you money. Real-time services are like that for the Internet.

sections.title: Specifying Performance Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC proposes three main performance metrics: delay, throughput, and reliability. Delay bounds can be deterministic (all packets arrive within 200 ms) or statistical (95 percent of packets arrive within 200 ms). Delay jitter is the variation in arrival times; for video, tight jitter bounds matter more than average delay. Throughput bounds are lower bounds (the network must deliver at least this many bits per second), and can also be statistical or average over a time interval.

Reliability is expressed as a probability of correct delivery. Clients can specify that they want 99 percent of messages to arrive uncorrupted. The RFC also covers other properties: messages should arrive in sequence, duplicates should be eliminated, the service should recover quickly from failures, and setup should be fast. Each client specifies its needs in a request; if the network cannot meet them, it rejects the request and explains why, so the client can modify and retry.
sections.eli5: The client says: I need all packets to arrive within 200 milliseconds, at least 1 megabit per second, and 99 percent of them must not be corrupted. The network says yes or no.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
Interactive voice (VOIP) needs a 200 millisecond delay bound and tight jitter (1 millisecond or less for good quality). Some packet loss can be tolerated (2 percent or so) because a lost voice packet does not ruin the conversation. Non-interactive video (like a recorded stream) needs high throughput (4.14 megabytes per second for HDTV at 30 frames per second) and tight jitter bounds (5 milliseconds), but can tolerate more packet loss (10 percent) because frames can be patched with old data.

Emergency alerts in a distributed real-time system need hard delay guarantees (50 milliseconds) and very high reliability (no retransmission, since retransmission is slow; use error-correcting codes instead). File transfers care most about throughput (minimum 728 kilobytes per second) and eventual reliability (100 percent, using retransmission if needed). Each application has different priorities.
sections.eli5: A voice call is like a conversation: you need fast response time but can handle a dropped word. A video stream is like watching a movie: you can pause for buffering but need smooth playback. A file transfer is like copying data: it must be perfect eventually.

sections.title: Translating Requirements Across Layers
sections.content:
A client's requirements start at the application layer and must be translated to lower protocol layers (TCP, IP, Ethernet). The RFC provides formulas for this translation. If a client specifies a 200 millisecond end-to-end delay bound and the application layer consumes 10 milliseconds, then the transport layer must deliver with a 190 millisecond bound. If messages are fragmented into smaller pieces, the delay bound for each fragment is reduced by the time gap between fragments.

For statistical bounds, the translation is more complex. A system can be pessimistic (assume any layer failure means the whole message fails) or optimistic (assume layer failures are independent). To guarantee the global bound, the pessimistic approach must be used. Throughput bounds increase as you go down the stack because lower layers add headers and encapsulation. Reliability bounds stay the same unless fragmentation increases the chance of losing a complete message.
sections.eli5: If your video player needs all frames to arrive in 1000 milliseconds, but the application layer takes 100 milliseconds to decode, the network has 900 milliseconds to deliver it.

sections.title: Open Questions
sections.content:
The RFC anticipates objections to the approach. One is that guarantees are unnecessary if networks have enough bandwidth. The RFC replies that history shows bandwidth is always in demand, and limited resources require allocation policies. Another objection is that reserving resources (to provide guarantees) is wasteful. The RFC suggests using priorities and preemption instead: real-time traffic preempts best-effort traffic as needed, so the network can serve both without exclusive reservations.

A third objection is that delay bounds are not necessary if throughput is guaranteed. The RFC responds that throughput and delay are independent metrics; you can have high throughput and high delay. Others argue that statistical bounds are unverifiable. The RFC agrees and suggests fractional bounds (out of 100 consecutive packets, 97 must be on time) instead of probabilities.
sections.eli5: Some people said: guarantees are not necessary because networks will be fast. Or: guarantees are too expensive. Or: delay does not matter if you have enough bandwidth. The RFC argues for all three and explains why.

items.title: Delay
items.text: Maximum time for a message to arrive, e.g., 200 ms

items.title: Jitter
items.text: Variation in delay, e.g., +/- 5 ms around the target
